background.definition: Delirium is a disturbance of consciousness characterized by a reduced ability to focus, sustain, or shift attention. The change in cognition is not better accounted for by a preexisting dementia. The disturbance develops within hours to days, and fluctuates throughout the day. It is caused by the direct physiologic consequences of a general medical condition.

list.listitem: Twenty percent of hospitalized elderly more than 65 years develop delirium.
Up to 50% of high-risk patients develop this condition while hospitalized.
More than 70% of patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting develop this condition.
Healthcare expenditure for delirium is estimated to be greater than $145 billion per year
Average increase in length of stay due to delirium is 8 days.
Causes are multiple, and frequently more than one underlying cause contributes to delirium.
Dementia, poor functional status, visual impairment, and older than 65 years are some common patient factors.
Environmental stressors include infection, anticholinergic or narcotic drugs, systemic glucocorticoids, and use of restraints.
Use of perioperative gabapentin in patients 65 years and older is associated with an increased likelihood of delirium following major surgery (RR 1.3).

In an open label randomized trial with 2634 patients, patients randomized to cefipime had a higher risk of coma or delirium at day 14 than those given piperacillin-tazobactam (20.8% vs 17.3%, p < 0.05, NNT = 29).
See .
Delirium is not well understood.
A combination of cholinergic deficiency, dopamine excess, decreased cerebral perfusion, and inflammation is felt to be involved.
Once the process is triggered, a complex cascade of events occurs, resulting in delirium.
One-third of delirium cases can be prevented by reducing risk factors: cognitive impairment, sleep deprivation, immobility, visual impairment, hearing impairment, and dehydration. B
Successful educational interventions to improve recognition of delirium are interactive, engage leadership, and use clinical pathways or assessment tools.
Nurses should be trained to recognize that delirium, dementia, and depression present with overlapping clinical features and may coexist in the older adult.
Nurses should be trained to be aware of the differences in the clinical features of delirium, dementia, and depression and use a structured assessment method to facilitate this process.
Clinicians should maintain high index of suspicion for delirium, depression, and dementia in the elderly, recognizing that these conditions may overlap.
Clinicians should screen patients for changes in cognition, function, behavior, and or mood using standardized tools to substantiate clinical observations.
In high-risk patients, an intervention addressing 6 factors reduced the risk of first episode of delirium from 15% to 10% (NNT = 20), as well as days and total episodes of delirium.
These 6 factors are: (1) cognitive impairment, (2) sleep deprivation, (3) immobility, (4) visual impairment, (5) hearing impairment, and (6) dehydration.

A systematic review and meta-analysis that included the above study found similar effectiveness of other multicomponent interventions in reducing the risk of delirium (NNT = 16) and decreasing falls. A Cochrane review containing 39 RCTs also supported multicomponent interventions, and found no clear evidence that cholinesterase inhibitors, melatonin, or antipsychotic medications reduce the risk of delirium in hospitalized non-ICU patients.

Perioperative melatonin (3 mg daily starting 2 days prior to major cardiac surgery and continuing for 7 days after surgery) did not reduce the risk of delirium in a RCT of 202 adults older than 50 years.
In a RCT, delirium-free ICU patients who received prophylactic haloperidol were not less likely to develop delirium, and length of stay and survival were no different than the placebo group.
A systematic review of RCTs found no benefit of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics in preventing delirium in hospitalized patients.

In a RCT, mechanically ventilated adults with sepsis who were being treated with light-sedation approaches, outcomes (including delirium free survival) did not differ between patients who received dexmedetomidine and patients who received propofol.
A systematic review and meta-analysis did not show sufficient evidence to support electroencephalography-guided anesthetic delivery for preventing postoperative delirium in adults.
The diagnosis of delirium is missed in up to 70% of affected patients. B
All ill elderly should undergo cognitive assessment. C
A thorough evaluation to determine the underlying cause of delirium is required. C
Neuroimaging studies are usually not indicated in diagnosing delirium. C
Typical patient presents with onset over hours to days; symptoms come and go, with lucid moments in between.
Speech and conversation may be disorganized.
Memory deficits and hallucinations are common, as well as agitation, lethargy, or both. Sleep cycle is often disturbed and emotions may be labile with fear, paranoia, anxiety, or irritability.
Begin by establishing baseline level of cognition and function.
Look for clues to underlying etiologies, such as a history of head trauma, new medications, alcohol intake, and presence of fever.
A validated predictive modelcan place patients in to low, medium, or high risk of developing delirium.

Delirium can present with hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed subtypes. The hypoactive type is most common, and physical signs may be subtle. The hyperactive form is easier to identify, as patients are agitated, delusional, or disoriented.
Delirium is a clinical diagnosis.
Delirium may be the only sign of a serious condition.
All patients should undergo evaluation to search for the cause of delirium (see section on Approach to the Patient below).
Neuroimaging is not generally recommended unless there is a history of head trauma, concern of CNS infection, or in a patient who presents with delirium and no other history is available.

The confusion assessment method (CAM) is recommended by US guidelines for the diagnosis of delirium. This model has 4 criteria: (1) acute onset and fluctuating course, (2) presence of inattention, (3) disorganized thinking, and (4) altered level of consciousness. To diagnose delirium, the first 2 criteria are required, with either one of the last 2 criteria present.
A systematic review found the CAM to be the most accurate diagnostic tool that could be performed in less than 5 minutes, with similar accuracy when performed by a physician or a nurse.

The CAM-S, a 4-item short form or 10-item long form derived from the CAM, predicts delirium severity and has been correlated with outcomes such as length of hospital stay and likelihood of death or nursing home placement.
A systematic review with 1350 patients in 7 studies found that the 3 minute CAM was 92% sensitive and 95% specific overall (LR+ 18, LR- 0.08).
A validated predictive modelcan place patients in to low, medium, or high risk of developing delirium.
High-risk patients have an 80% chance of developing delirium (see ).

The Ottawa 3DYear risk score has been well validated and is highly sensitive for the detection of cognitive impairment in older patients in the emergency department. It consists of four questions: what is the day, what is the date, spell world backwards, and what is the year; 1 or more errors constitutes a positive test (90% sensitive, 61% specific, LR+ 2.3, LR- 0.17).
The 4AT score is another validated risk score for identifying patients with delirium in the ED, with sensitivity and specificity of approximately 88%.
Look for underlying causes of delirium if present.

For physiologic etiologies, perform the following: chemistries, thyroid function tests, electrocardiogram, urinalysis, oxygen saturation/arterial blood gas, chest x-ray, and evaluate for fecal impaction.
For history-related factors, check the following: all medications, alcohol use, fever or symptoms of infection, postoperative state, hepatic or renal disease, ICU admission or critical illness.
Evaluate for other causes of confusion, such as psychiatric disorders, substance abuse, neurovascular insult, dementia without delirium.
Treatment requires addressing the underlying cause of delirium. C
Reducing risk factors can improve cognition. A
Supportive care is a large part of the treatment of delirium. B
Physical restraints should be discouraged. A

Antipsychotic drugs have not been shown to be more effective than placebo for prevention or treatment of delirium, except for brexpiprazole for the treatment of agitation in patients with Alzheimer's dementia., , , A
For patients with comorbid dementia, ramelteon and dextromethorphan-quinidine may be effective based on single trials. B
Nonpharmacologic treatment has a large role in treatment ().

A systematic review of medications for agitation in the ED found that severely agitated elderly patients are at high risk of adverse effects when given medications for acute agitation. The adverse events are especially more likely with benzodiazepines, especially midazolam.

Brexipiprazole is FDA approved for the treatment of agitation in patients due to Alzheimer's disease, the first medication approved for this indication, based on two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trials. Patients with probable Alzheimer's disease based on Mini Mental Status Exam (MMSE) between 5 and 22 who received brexpiprazole had a clinically significant reduction in their Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory (CMAI) total scores compared to placebo at the end of 12 weeks. However, there is still a 'black box' warning for medications of this class for increased mortality when used to treat psychosis caused by dementia.

A randomized trial of 135 patients undergoing noncardiac thoracic surgery randomized them to haloperidol 0.5 mg tid or placebo. Overall, the rate of delirium in haloperidol-treated patients was similar (22%) to the rate in placebo-treated patients (28%). Among those who developed delirium, haloperidol did not delay its onset, shorten its duration, or lessen its severity. Additionally, the patients taking haloperidol did not have shorter hospitalizations or time in the ICU.

A randomized trial with 566 patients compared haloperidol, ziprasidone and placebo in patients with acute respiratory failure or shock who develop delirium in the ICU. The use of haloperidol or ziprasidone did not reduce the duration of delirium. This trial was powered to detect at least a 2-day difference in the duration of delirium, so a smaller difference cannot be excluded.

Investigators randomized 732 delirium-free patients who were expected to stay in the ICU for at least 2 days to receive either 1 mg of haloperidol every 8 hours, 2 mg of haloperidol every 8 hours, or matching placebo IV. Survival in the 2 mg haloperidol group and the placebo group were similar: 83% at 28 days and 79% at 90 days in both groups. The number of delirium-free days, duration of mechanical ventilation, and ICU and hospital lengths of stay were also similar between groups.

A systematic review of 14 RCTs evaluated antipsychotics compared with each other or placebo for prevention of delirium. Haloperidol was not effective. While there is some evidence that second-generation antipsychotics can reduce delirium incidence in the post-operative setting (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26-0.50), these drugs have no effect on hospital LOS or mortality and there is insufficient evidence to determine effect on delirium severity, delirium duration, or sedation.

In a similarly conducted systematic review evaluating the use of antipsychotics for the treatment of delirium in hospitalized patients, 16 RCTs and 10 observational studies (n=5607) were included. Haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics, as compared with placebo, did not affect delirium duration, mortality, sedation status, or hospital LOS. Second-generation antipsychotic use did, however, result in more harmful cardiac effects, specifically QT prolongation, as compared with placebo (RR 1.95, 95% CI 1.03-3.71).
Benzodiazepines have not been shown to be helpful in the treatment of non-alcohol withdrawal related delirium.
A randomized trial with 120 hospitalized patients 65 and older with dilirium found no benefit for melatonin.
In adults with delirium plus pyuria or asymptomatic bacteruria, a systematic review found 4 low quality studies concluding that antibiotics are not helpful.
Haloperidol may be preferred for terminally ill patients with delirium (over chlorpromazine and lorazepam).

A randomized trial found with 90 patients found that a single dose of lorazepam in combination with haloperidol decreases agitation in end-of-life cancer patients with persistent agitated delirium despite scheduled haloperidol.

In an RCT of 97 hospitalized patients with delirium on admission, long-acting intranasal insulin decreased the duration of delirium by a clinically meaningful, but not statistically significant, 2 days in hospitalized older adults. For those younger than 88 years, intranasal insulin decreased delirium duration by 3 days. This is promising, but larger studies are needed, especially to determine the potential harms.

A network meta-analysis of 59 trials with 15,781 patients concluded that the following drugs were most effective for psychotic symptoms in patients with dementia: For reducing psychosis, surprisingly, donepezil was the most effective (SMD -0.31), haloperidol was next (-0.27), then aripiprazole (-0.22), and risperidone (-0.15).

A trial randomized 204 patients with agitation and dementia in outpatients to mirtazapine or placebo, with a target dose of 45 mg daily of mirtazapine. There was no difference in levels of agitation at 12 weeks, and there were numerically more deaths in the mirtazapine group (7 vs 1).

A randomized trial with 220 patients found that dextromethorphan-quinidine (Nuedexta) may be useful for reducing agitation and aggressive behavior in adults with Alzheimer disease dementia. How clinicially significant the treatment differences are and whether the results will persist longer than 10 weeks remain unclear.

In this small, single-blinded study (n=63) ramelteon was shown to be effective in preventing delirium in elderly patients who required hospitalization for acute illness. You would have to treat 3 patients with ramelteon to prevent one episode of delirium.
Educational interventions can reduce the duration of delirium, length of hospital stay, and time in a skilled nursing facility.
Caregivers should reduce environmental factors that may contribute, including isolation of patient and chaotic workplace.

A systematic review of multicomponent interventions for the prevention of delirium found 7 studies with about 1700 patients. The found that multicomponent interventions, as heterogeneous as they are, decrease the rate of delirium in hospitalized elderly patients (NNT=16) and decrease falls (NNT=14). They don't, however, have any effect on length of stay or survival.
Caregivers should avoid, if at all possible, chemical and physical restraints.

In acute inpatient wards, a cluster randomized trial found that the implementation of a program promoting mobility, nutrition/hydration, and cognitive engagement for older hospitalized patients decreased the incidence of delirium. However, it did not reduce length of stay nor improve hospital-associated disability, incontinence, falls, or pressure injuries.

For elderly, postoperative patients still in the hospital, a Chinese RCT with 281 patients found that asking family members and caregivers to deliver interventions intended to prevent delirium decreases the risk of postoperative delirium (POD). The active participation of family members was an essential factor of this program and may not be feasible in places where this is not the cultural norm.

Avoid perioperative gabapentin for pain control. Use of perioperative gabapentin in patients 65 years and older is associated with an increased likelihood of delirium following major surgery (RR 1.3).
The majority of patients either present to the hospital with delirium, or develop delirium while hospitalized.
No benefit occurred with the use of a consulting service versus standard care.
Delirious patients are at risk for aspiration, decubitus ulcers, and nosocomial infections due to prolonged immobilization and increased length of hospital stay.
See .
In hospital, mortality rate is 22% to 76%; 1 year mortality is 35% to 40% (RR = 3). B
Delirium often takes weeks to months to resolve, and 40% required nursing home placement. B
Functional and cognitive decline at 12 months is significantly greater in patients with delirium compared with similarly matched control patients. B
One-third of patients with delirium will not return to baseline cognition. B
Delirium in persons age 65 years and older is associated with increased risks of institutionalization and dementia. B
None recommended.
Delirium is uncommon in children.
